definition: Retract means to withdraw a statement, promise, or claim, especially because it was found to be wrong.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word retract. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know retract should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The newspaper had to retract its front-page report once documents proved the local factory had actually passed its safety inspection.
To qualify a statement is weaker — you soften it or add conditions while still standing behind it, instead of retracting it outright.
To abjure is stronger — it is a solemn, often sworn renouncing of a belief entirely, going beyond retracting one mistaken statement.

Withdraw means to pull back or take back something offered or stated — a bid, an application, a remark — and it is the general word for any pulling-back. Retract is the pointed version: you take back a specific public statement or claim because it proved wrong. You can withdraw an offer that was perfectly sound; a retraction admits error.

Rescind means to officially cancel a decision, offer, or rule — a company rescinds a job offer, a board rescinds a policy. What gets rescinded is an act with legal or official force. Retract applies to things said or published: statements, claims, and testimony taken back as mistaken.

Recant means to formally give up a belief or position one once professed, classically under pressure — heretics were made to recant. Retract is narrower and factual: you take back a particular statement or claim because it turned out to be wrong, with no change of creed required.

Retract means to withdraw a statement, promise, or claim, especially because it was found to be wrong.
After an outside team found a critical error in the lab's measurements, the chemist chose to retract the paper rather than defend a flawed result.

Retract fits because the chemist is formally taking back a published claim — the paper — specifically because it was discovered to be wrong, which is the word's core situation in science and publishing.
Retract is the standard word in journalism, science, and law — newspapers retract stories, researchers retract papers, witnesses retract testimony.
It also keeps its literal 'pull back' sense (a cat retracts its claws).
In casual conversation, people usually say 'take back' instead.

In her acclaimed history of the Aldwyn shipyard, Dr.
Ferris wrote that the company had hidden a 1911 fire from its investors.
The claim was repeated in reviews, quoted in documentaries, and taught in at least one university course.
Then a graduate student located the shipyard's original ledger, which showed the fire had been reported to investors within a week.
Ferris did not hesitate: in the next printing she moved to retract the claim, and the publisher inserted a note calling the passage an error.
Colleagues praised the correction; as one put it, a historian's authority rests less on never erring than on what she does when the record proves her wrong.
